Question: A \(6\)-inch-diameter pole and an \(18\)-inch-diameter pole are placed together and bound together with wire. The length of the shortest wire that will go around them is:
Solution:
Use the usual model of touching circular cross-sections, with a negligibly thin wire wrapped around them in one perpendicular plane. Their radii are \(3\) and \(9\) inches. A shortest enclosing wire is taut: any free bend or inward detour can be shortened. It therefore follows two outer common tangent segments and the exposed circular arcs, joining the arcs tangentially.

Let \(O\) and \(P\) be the centers of the smaller and larger circles, respectively. Since the circles touch, \(OP=3+9=12\). Let \(A\) and \(B\) be the contact points of one outer tangent on the smaller and larger circles. Both contact radii are perpendicular to \(AB\).

Draw through \(O\) a line parallel to \(AB\), meeting \(PB\) at \(H\). The resulting right triangle \(OPH\) has
\[
PH=9-3=6,\qquad OH=AB.
\]
The Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
AB=\sqrt{12^2-6^2}=6\sqrt3.
\]
The other tangent segment has the same length by reflection across \(OP\).

To find the arc angles without trigonometry, reflect \(P\) across \(OH\) to a point \(P'\). Then \(PP'=2PH=12\), and \(OP'=OP=12\). Thus \(OPP'\) is equilateral, giving \(\angle OPH=60^\circ\).

The two contact radii on the larger circle are reflections across \(OP\), so they enclose \(120^\circ\) on the side facing the smaller circle. The wire uses the remaining \(240^\circ\) arc. The corresponding contact radii on the smaller circle are parallel to those on the larger circle, and its exposed arc, facing away from the larger circle, has angle \(120^\circ\).

Adding the two straight segments and both exposed arcs gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
L&=2(6\sqrt3)
 +\frac{120}{360}(2\pi\cdot3)
 +\frac{240}{360}(2\pi\cdot9)\\
 &=12\sqrt3+14\pi.
\end{aligned}
\]
The shortest wire is therefore \(\boxed{12\sqrt3+14\pi\text{ inches}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
